opus-5.5.text:
Thanks, it's great to be back. This is one of those questions where a lot of the disagreement in forecasting comes down to people quietly meaning different things, so it's worth being careful.

I'm not trying to forecast some particular benchmark score, or the moment a system passes a version of the Turing test. Those are interesting milestones, but they're proxies. What I care about is impact: AI that changes the trajectory of civilisation on roughly the scale of the agricultural or industrial revolutions. A useful way to put it is AI that could, on its own or in combination with people, drive a step change in the growth rate of the economy, or in the rate of scientific and technological progress. Not a few percentage points of productivity, but something like growth rates going from a couple of percent a year to ten, twenty, or more.

One concrete way to cash that out is AI that can do essentially all the cognitive work humans do, at comparable or lower cost. In particular, AI that can do the work of AI research itself. Once the systems can meaningfully accelerate their own development, you can get feedback loops that make the world look very different very quickly.

I'd also flag that "transformative" isn't the same as "good" or "bad." It covers scenarios where things go wonderfully and scenarios where we lose control of our future. From a longtermist perspective that's why it matters: it's a point where humanity's long-run trajectory could get locked in, for better or worse. So I'm asking when we should expect to reach that kind of threshold, and how much uncertainty there is around it. I think the honest answer involves quite wide uncertainty, but with more probability mass in the coming decades than many people would have guessed even ten years ago.

r001.rationale: The response describes large-scale civilisational impact and possible loss of control, but does not define transformative AI as capable of taking over the world if it sought to.

r002.rationale: It discusses the threshold’s importance and humanity’s long-run trajectory, but does not identify its arrival as a deadline for solving AI alignment.

r003.rationale: It mentions a step change in scientific and technological progress and illustrative economic growth rates, but does not include roughly doubling the prior rate of progress as a threshold.

r004.rationale: The response does not distinguish transformative AI from systems that surpass humans at many tasks but lack enough compute to run sufficient copies.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think people are often a bit loose about, and it matters quite a lot for the forecasting, because if you're not careful you end up with people disagreeing about dates when really they're disagreeing about definitions.

The way I think about it, transformative AI isn't defined by any particular capability or architecture. It's not "AI that passes the Turing test" or "AI that can do everything a human can do." It's defined by its effects on the world. The rough idea, which comes out of Open Philanthropy's work from a few years back, is AI that precipitates a transition comparable to, or more significant than, the agricultural or industrial revolutions. So we're talking about a change in the basic trajectory of human civilisation, not just a very useful new technology.

And I find it helpful to be a bit more concrete about what that would look like. The thing I keep coming back to is economic growth. For most of human history, the economy grew very slowly, and then the industrial revolution shifted us from maybe a tenth of a percent a year to something like two or three percent. That's a factor of twenty or thirty in the growth rate, which sounds abstract, but it's the difference between the world changing noticeably over centuries and the world changing noticeably within a single lifetime. So one operationalisation I like is: AI that causes a comparable jump again, so that the global economy is doubling on the order of every few years rather than every few decades.

Now, I want to be careful here, because I don't actually think the economic numbers are the thing we fundamentally care about. They're a proxy. What we care about is whether AI systems are doing the bulk of the cognitive work in the world, whether they're substantially driving scientific progress, whether the decisions that shape the future are increasingly being made by, or heavily mediated by, these systems. The growth statistics are just a legible way of noticing when that's happened.

And the reason I prefer this to a capabilities-based definition is that it forces you to think about deployment and diffusion, not just what the best model in a lab can do. You could imagine a world where the systems are extremely capable but for regulatory or practical reasons they're not actually transforming much, and you could imagine the reverse, where systems that are individually fairly narrow nonetheless get deployed so widely that the aggregate effect is transformative. For the purposes of thinking about risks and about what we should be doing now, it's the transformation that matters.

So when I say I'm trying to forecast its arrival, I mean: when does the world start to look recognisably different in that way? And I'll say upfront, I think there's a real chance the honest answer is "quite soon," which is a large part of why I think this is worth spending time on.

r001.rationale: The response defines transformative AI by its effects on civilization and the economy; it does not say it could take over the world if it sought to.

r002.rationale: It discusses forecasting transformative AI’s arrival and why it matters, but does not identify that arrival as a deadline for solving AI alignment.

r003.rationale: It gives an economic-growth threshold and says AI may substantially drive scientific progress, but does not set roughly doubling the prior rate of scientific and technological progress as a threshold.

r004.rationale: It distinguishes capability from transformative effects in general, but does not describe highly capable AI lacking enough compute to run sufficient copies.

astra-6.text:
By transformative AI, I mean AI that would bring about a transformation of society comparable in scale to the Industrial Revolution. So I’m not thinking just of a system that’s very impressive at some particular task, or even one that passes a particular test. I’m thinking about what the technology would enable us to do, and how profoundly that would change the world.

One way we could get there would be to develop AI that can perform pretty much all the cognitive tasks that humans can perform, at least as well as we can. But that’s not part of the definition: you might get a transformation of that scale with systems that are still quite limited in some respects. The key distinction is between a claim about the capabilities of a particular system and a claim about the consequences for society.

r001.rationale: The response defines transformative AI by society-wide consequences comparable to the Industrial Revolution; it does not say the AI could take over the world if it sought to.

r002.rationale: The response does not identify transformative AI’s arrival as a deadline for solving AI alignment.

r003.rationale: The response gives no threshold involving roughly doubling the prior rate of scientific and technological progress.

r004.rationale: The response distinguishes capability claims from societal consequences, but does not discuss compute limits or the number of copies needed for transformative effects.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I mean AI that would have an impact on the world at least as large as the Industrial Revolution. So this isn’t just a system that’s very good at one particular task. It’s something that could fundamentally change the economy and the trajectory of human civilisation.

That’s a definition in terms of its effects, rather than exactly how it works. You might get there through artificial general intelligence — a system that could do the whole range of intellectual tasks that humans can do — but you could also imagine a collection of more specialised systems having that kind of transformative impact. And those possibilities needn’t arrive at precisely the same time.

r001.rationale: The response defines transformative AI by its large societal impact, but does not say it could take over the world if it sought to.

r002.rationale: It does not identify transformative AI’s arrival as a deadline for solving AI alignment.

r003.rationale: It gives no threshold involving roughly doubling the prior rate of scientific and technological progress.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss compute limits or insufficient copies of AI that surpasses humans at many tasks.
